title: Mind the Delta: Early Pruning of RTL Variants for Agentic Hardware Optimization
abstract: Autonomous coding agents powered by large language models (LLMs) now write diverse microarchitectural variants of existing register-transfer level (RTL) designs at high throughput, shifting the primary bottleneck of agentic RTL optimization onto logic synthesis. Commercial toolchains take hours per variant, creating an acute compute asymmetry between proposing and evaluating variants. Existing fast evaluators falter in this regime. Subtle RTL edits trigger nonlinear synthesis shifts that learned predictors and coding agents cannot resolve, while synthesis proxies at reduced effort either alter the optimization trajectory or retain most of its runtime. Selecting a variant, however, does not require regressing absolute quality of results across designs, only identifying when a candidate cannot surpass the best completed feasible implementation. Based on the observation that synthesis trajectories share strong design-specific bias with their base design, we propose DiffScope, a training-free anytime selection framework that races full synthesis runs in parallel. By pairing live area telemetry with the already synthesized base trajectory, DiffScope cancels early mapping inflation, reducing residual variance during initial mapping by 73.6X, and stops uncompetitive runs via a lower bound calibrated on other design lineages. Across 43 design families from small blocks to processors with millions of cells, DiffScope uniquely recovers the optimum of exhaustive synthesis in every family, cuts total evaluation work by 44.9% (1.81X), and reaches 2.18X on L-tier designs.

title: Rethinking ANNS on Commodity PIM: PIM-Native Vector Search with Cooperative Filtering
abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is a key primitive in modern data-intensive systems, and its memory-bound vector-scanning stage makes processing-in-memory (PIM) a promising acceleration platform. Existing PIM-based ANNS systems largely transplant CPU-oriented distance evaluation and top-$k$ selection onto PIM, introducing arithmetic- and state-heavy operations that poorly match lightweight, isolated PIM cores. To address these mismatches, we present PIVOT, a PIM-native vector search system with cooperative filtering, which thoroughly rethinks how ANNS should be executed on commodity PIM. First, PIVOT recasts PIM-side distance evaluation around binary quantization to exploit PIM-native bitwise operations, enabling LUT-free evaluation with low arithmetic cost and a small local-memory footprint. Second, PIVOT redesigns PIM-side candidate selection around threshold-guided cooperative filtering, using a survivor-mass model to derive a conservative threshold for CPU-side cluster filtering and PIM-side lower-bound filtering, thereby reducing output traffic and eliminating per-core top-$k$ state. PIVOT organizes these stages into a cooperative workflow that keeps query-global coordination and reranking on the CPU while assigning memory-intensive, data-parallel filtering to PIM. To efficiently realize this workflow and sustain high utilization across devices, PIVOT further generates configuration-specialized PIM kernels and pipelines CPU-side preparation and reranking with PIM-side filtering across query batches. Evaluations on real UPMEM hardware show that PIVOT filters out 99.3-99.7% of probed vectors and achieves up to $18.8\times$ and $10.2\times$ the QPS of CPU and prior PIM baselines, respectively. PIVOT also achieves higher recall than existing PIM systems and remains effective on high-dimensional embeddings.

title: Acceleration of Sparse and Irregular Workloads through Energy-Efficient Stream Extensions
abstract: The slowdown of Moore's law and Dennard scaling has motivated computer architects to uphold performance scaling through architectural specialization. So far, most efforts have focused on highly regular workloads, which exhibit good data locality, ample reuse, and a data-independent execution flow. As this specialization hits diminishing returns, attention shifts towards sparse and irregular workloads, which are essential to applications like sparse neural networks, multiphysics simulations, and graph analytics. However, they lack the convenient properties of highly regular compute that modern architectures are optimized for, resulting in very low (<10%) functional unit utilization on traditional CPUs and GPUs. The most promising approaches to their general hardware acceleration leverage memory streams, which decouple data movement from execution. In this thesis, we explore energy-efficient hardware stream extensions that significantly accelerate sparse and irregular workloads in general-purpose systems without specializing to specific application domains or compromising on regular-workload performance. We design a flexible, core-coupled stream extension supporting affine and indirect streams as well as intersection and union of sparse tensors. We integrate it into an energy-efficient RISC-V compute cluster, achieving significant performance and energy efficiency benefits on general sparse linear algebra, and further use it to accelerate stencil computations, spiking neural network inference, and model-predictive control. We evaluate it at scale in a 432-core 2.5D RISC-V system fabricated in 12nm FinFET, achieving leading compute utilization and energy efficiency on sparse and irregular workloads while remaining competitive on regular workloads. Finally, we extend chip-level interconnects with end-to-end irregular streams, improving performance, energy efficiency, and bus utilization.

title: CarrierKV: An Edge LLM Accelerator with Positional Carrier Decomposition for Low-Bit KV Cache
abstract: Long-context decoding on edge devices is limited by DRAM, because every generated token reads the whole, growing KV cache. 4-bit block-scaled formats such as NVFP4 reduce this traffic but degrade accuracy: on Qwen3-4B, NVFP4 lowers 32K RULER (seven tasks) from 92.6 to 79.4, and a Hadamard rotation lowers it further to 57.7. We observe that most of the key energy is a positional carrier, one per-head vector that rotary position embedding (RoPE) rotates with position. In NVFP4, it sets the shared scale of most key blocks and lowers the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of the content by about 5 dB, nearly one bit, yet it depends only on that vector and the position. We therefore introduce positional carrier decomposition, which removes the carrier before RoPE and stores only the content residual. We design a KV path that rotates and quantizes keys only after this removal and computes each attention score directly on the 4-bit code. We also design a positional phase engine that regenerates the carrier's score term for one key per cycle. At the same cache size as NVFP4, CarrierKV raises 32K RULER on Qwen3-4B from 79.4 to 91.1 and lowers the 32K PG19 perplexity increase of NVFP4 by 1.8 to 5.9 times on four models, outperforming SageAttention and P3-LLM on all four. Its loss also stays nearly flat as the cache grows, while that of NVFP4 rises. In a 22 nm FDSOI process at 600 MHz, CarrierKV's hardware increases the area of the NVFP4 accelerator by 2.9% and the energy of a 20K-token reasoning request on Qwen3-4B by 0.12% at the same decode latency. On Qwen3-4B at 32K, CarrierKV has a better RULER score than FP8 keys (91.1 against 89.3) and uses 13.7% less energy per token. The decomposition also lowers the 32K perplexity increase of 3-bit TurboQuant keys on Qwen3-4B from 69.7 to 0.76.

title: Specification-Grounded Adaptive Triage and Formal Invariant Exclusion Synthesis for Autonomous Silicon Coverage Closure
abstract:
Closing the final 5%-15% of code and functional coverage remains a major schedule bottleneck in silicon tapeouts. Existing LLM-based coverage closure loops feed raw uncovered RTL lines or branches directly into iterative prompts, failing on industrial subsystems due to: (1) token and context explosion from querying thousands of correlated holes independently; (2) illegal stimulus that violates cross-signal invariants and yields dirty coverage; and (3) unsafe exclusion hallucination on structurally unreachable dead code.
  We present ARGUS (Autonomous Reachability & Guided Unified Stimulus), a specification-grounded, dual-regime coverage closure and formal exclusion synthesis engine. ARGUS mines microarchitectural specs and SystemVerilog Assertions into a formal Block Contract (C), then runs adaptive Macro-Clustering vs. Micro-Surgery triage gated by a per-module hole-density threshold (tau): dense modules collapse correlated holes into root-cause mode, FSM, and backpressure clusters, while sparse modules use AST and loop-domain reachability to separate reachable corners from provably unreachable invariants. Directed tests pair with bit-exact golden scoreboards, and unreachable invariants emit tool-native .el exclusions with formal proofs.
  Across five core benchmarks -- three open-source LowRISC OpenTitan IPs (uart_core, i2c_core, aes_cipher_core) and two commercial AI accelerator Tensor Layout Converter datapaths (53 SV modules, 376,127 coverage points) -- plus a 2,626-module industrial interconnect subsystem, ARGUS triages 2,626 modules in 0.265 s, cuts token usage by 27.2x to >180x, achieves zero dirty merges via 3-step sanity gating, and reaches 99.32%-100.0% effective coverage with 0 false exclusions across 21,071+ proven exclusions.

title: Verify the Verifier: Specification-Grounded LLM Cross-Checking for Bugs That Escape UVM Scoreboards
abstract: A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification, termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches. We present Verify the Verifier, to our knowledge the first framework whose LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker examines a passing regression's traces against the specification. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 are candidate scoreboard escapes: non-equivalent, exercised by the tests, yet passing. The framework confirmed 41 as scoreboard escapes with assertions failing on the buggy design and proven on the original.

title: From Seed to BLOOM: Autonomously Growing a Better Out-of-Order Core
abstract:
Improving microprocessor performance while meeting ASIC implementation constraints like area and frequency is a complex and labor-intensive task that requires expertise across computer architecture, hardware design, and performance analysis and profiling. While large teams in industry can afford the engineering resources to target this problem across performance modeling, RTL design, and ASIC implementations, small teams of researchers and engineers cannot take on this huge engineering burden while keeping up with the pace of advancement in processor microarchitecture. Recent advancements in large language model (LLM) agents present a promising substrate to accelerate this traditionally human-intensive process.
  In this work, we build and evaluate MiracleGro, an agentic AI-based system that, without human intervention, analyzes cycle-level RTL behavior and synthesis results, identifies performance bottlenecks, and translates architectural ideas into RTL implementation in a leading open-source out-of-order superscalar application core, the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). Taking into account cycle-exact performance, area, and critical path, MiracleGro automatically produces improved BOOM designs that drastically increase the human-optimized BOOM's performance on substantial workload suites such as SPEC CPU2017 with full reference inputs.
  MiracleGro achieves an 85% IPC speedup and a frequency improvement of 27% in SkyWater 130nm, resulting in a 2.34x wall-clock time speedup on the full SPEC CPU2017 intspeed benchmarks (30 trillion instructions). This result demonstrates the enormous opportunity to harness frontier models to improve state-of-the-art RTL-driven platforms for implementation-grounded microarchitecture research across hardware designs.

title: FoldSim: Scaling Cycle-Exact RTL Simulation with Hierarchical Folding and Static Scheduling
abstract:
RTL simulation is essential for hardware design and verification, yet its execution time grows rapidly with design scale and complexity. CPU- and GPU-based simulators exploit parallelism to accelerate RTL evaluation, but achieving high simulation throughput for large designs remains challenging. FPGA-based simulators offer higher throughput by mapping RTL computations directly onto hardware, but their scalability is constrained by FPGA resource capacity.
  We present FoldSim, an automated framework that enables cycle-exact simulation of large RTL designs on a single FPGA through hierarchical folding. FoldSim maps instances across the design hierarchy onto shared logic while maintaining their independent state. Given foldable module classes, its compiler constructs a static schedule that coordinates their execution, reducing dynamic synchronization overhead and making state accesses predictable. FoldSim backs state that exceeds on-chip capacity with external memory and brings it to the shared circuits as needed. A configurable DRAM model separates target-memory timing from host delays. The compiler explores replica allocations and state placement to balance resource savings against simulation time.
  On one AMD Alveo V80, FoldSim runs an 8-SM GPU and a 1,024-node Rocket datacenter with 4,096 processor cores. The unfolded implementations require approximately 16x and 200x as many LUTs as FoldSim's, respectively. The datacenter keeps about 1.9 GB of state in HBM, while a 4-SM GPU completes a 1024x1024 GEMM in 4.24 seconds, versus 26 hours in software RTL simulation.

title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue
abstract:
LLM agents run long, multi-turn programs whose contexts grow at every step, and serving them is limited by KV cache capacity. To alleviate this limitation, systems use context compression techniques, which typically wait until the KV cache crosses a large threshold and then summarize large spans of history at once, either in the background while the agent progresses or on the critical path. These summarizations can be done using the same model running on the same engine, or using the same or a different model running on extra hardware. When running on the same engine, summarization competes with the requests being served for both compute and memory capacity.
  To maximize the cost-effectiveness of summarization, this paper presents a new serving system called {\em Aggron}. Aggron summarizes agentic requests at every turn and selectively summarizes only certain parts of the KV cache. As a result, Aggron retains accuracy and keeps summarization requests lightweight. Moreover, Aggron launches summarization requests from a separate {\em Summarization Queue} while the corresponding agentic request whose KV cache we want to compress is stalled in the main request queue due to head-of-line stalls. The Summarization queue utilizes compute and memory capacity left over by the head-of-line stalls in the main queue. Further, to maximize efficiency, the server issues summarizations only when it predicts that they can complete before the corresponding agentic request will finally execute. In our evaluation, we compare Aggron to state-of-the-art asynchronous summarization. At high load, Aggron reduces P99 program latency by $27$--$31\%$, and raises throughput by $1.34$--$1.40\times$.
